The fs_result object

Source: vignettes/articles/fs-result.Rmd
fs-result.Rmd

Fourteen of featR’s sixteen functions return the same object, an fs_result. The two exceptions, fs_pca() and fs_svd(), do dimensionality reduction and return their own lists; the dimensionality reduction article covers them. fs_supervised() and fs_unsupervised() also have an output argument that can return the filtered data, a logical mask, or column indices instead; its default, "result", gives an fs_result.

The seven components

An fs_result is a plain list with seven elements, always in this order:

Element Type Meaning
selected character The features the method kept. It may be character(0), never NULL.
scores named numeric, data.frame, or NULL Per-feature scores. They are comparable within one method, not across methods.
method string What actually ran, for example "supervised_correlation" or "svm_linear".
task string "classification", "regression", or NA.
model object or NULL The fitted model, when the method fits one.
details named list Method-specific extras, documented on each help page.
call call The matched call. 
d <- data.frame(
  signal = c(1.1, 2.3, 2.9, 4.2, 5.1, 5.8, 7.2, 8.1),
  flip   = c(8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1),
  noise  = c(3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6),
  y      = 1:8
)
res <- fs_supervised(d, target = "y", threshold = 0.5)

str(unclass(res), max.level = 1, give.attr = FALSE)
#> List of 7
#>  $ selected: chr [1:2] "signal" "flip"
#>  $ scores  : Named num [1:3] 0.998 1 0.477
#>  $ method  : chr "supervised_correlation"
#>  $ task    : chr "regression"
#>  $ model   : NULL
#>  $ details :List of 7
#>  $ call    : language fs_supervised(data = d, target = "y", threshold = 0.5)

Reading a result

print() gives a compact overview:

res
#> <fs_result> supervised_correlation (regression)
#> Selected 2 of 3 features
#>   signal, flip
#> Details: mask, indices, filtered, threshold, direction, action, n_features (in $details)

The first line names the method and, in parentheses, the task. The second counts the kept features against the candidates, and the third lists the kept names, cut off after the first 10 (print(res, n = 20) shows more). A Model: line appears when the method stored a fitted model, and the last line names the elements of details, which are described under Value on each function’s help page.

summary() adds the call and a table of up to 20 scores (set n for more), ranked strongest first. An asterisk marks the features that were kept:

summary(res)
#> <fs_result> supervised_correlation (regression)
#> Selected 2 of 3 features
#>   signal, flip
#> Details: mask, indices, filtered, threshold, direction, action, n_features (in $details)
#> 
#> Call:
#>   fs_supervised(data = d, target = "y", threshold = 0.5)
#> 
#> Scores (3 features, ranked):
#>  feature  score selected
#>     flip 1.0000        *
#>   signal 0.9978        *
#>    noise 0.4775         
#> (* = selected)

Here scores is the absolute correlation with y. flip is a perfect negative correlation, so it scores 1 and ranks above signal (0.998). noise scores 0.48, just under the 0.5 threshold.

selected() is the stable accessor for the chosen names. Prefer it to res$selected in code you intend to keep:

selected(res)
#> [1] "signal" "flip"

What scores means, method by method

A correlation of 0.8 and a Boruta importance of 0.8 have nothing in common, so compare scores only within one method. The table gives the quantity each function reports and which direction is stronger.

Function scores Stronger is
fs_unsupervised() the chosen criterion per column: variance, MAD (on the standard-deviation scale), IQR, range, proportion missing, or number of distinct values; NA when undefined depends on the criterion and on direction
fs_correlation() each variable’s largest absolute correlation with any other variable; NA when none could be computed larger means more redundant
fs_supervised() absolute Pearson r for a numeric outcome, in [0, 1]; one-way ANOVA F for a categorical outcome, Inf for perfect separation; NA for a constant feature larger
fs_chi() p-value adjusted for multiple testing (Bonferroni by default); NA for a feature that could not be tested smaller
fs_infogain() information gain in bits, or the gain ratio with normalize = "gain_ratio"; sorted, largest first larger
fs_lasso() a data.frame with Variable, signed Coefficient, and AbsCoefficient, one row per design-matrix column, zeros included; standardized (coefficient times the column’s standard deviation) when standardize = TRUE, the default. Raw coefficients are in details$coefficients larger magnitude
fs_elastic() absolute coefficients at the winning alpha and lambda, on the scale of the columns the model saw (not standardized), zeros included; NULL for multinomial fits larger
fs_randomforest() permutation importance: mean decrease in accuracy, or mean increase in MSE for regression; divided by its standard error unless control$scale_importance = FALSE; NULL when control$importance = FALSE larger; negative means worse than a permuted copy
fs_mars() unscaled earth variable importance from caret::varImp(), one entry per original predictor; pruned predictors score 0, and a predictor the final model uses can score 0 or less; NULL if varImp() fails larger, but selected is the predictors in the final model, not a cut on the score
fs_recursivefeature() each candidate’s importance in the full-size fit (all candidates present), averaged over every resample; falls back to caret::varImp() when the function set records no per-resample importance larger
fs_svm() with SVM-RFE, the squared weight w^2 of each column in the first, full-feature linear SVM; with select_method = "rf_rfe", random-forest importance averaged over resamples; NULL when feature_select = FALSE larger
fs_boruta() median Boruta importance over the runs; NA for a feature with no importance history larger
fs_stepwise() one entry per retained term: the absolute t statistic, or the largest absolute t among a factor’s or interaction’s coefficients. Biased upward by the selection, so not valid for inference larger
fs_bayes() NULL: the method compares whole models, so there is no per-feature score not applicable

summary() ranks by these rules:

  • Smaller ranks first for fs_chi(), for fs_correlation(prune = TRUE) (which keeps the least redundant variables), and for fs_unsupervised() and fs_supervised() when the kept side is the low one (direction = "below" with action = "keep", or "above" with "remove").
  • fs_lasso() ranks by absolute coefficient. Every other method ranks by the signed value, so a negative permutation or Boruta importance ranks below a useful feature instead of above it.
  • For fs_mars() and fs_correlation(prune = TRUE), which do not select by a cut on the score, the selected features are listed first, each group in score order, so a kept feature is never ranked below a dropped one.

Design-matrix columns

Some methods expand each factor or character predictor into one column per level and then score and select those columns. A factor color then shows up under its level columns, and you have to map them back yourself if you want the original variables.

  • fs_lasso() and fs_elastic() paste the level onto the name: colorgreen, colorred.
  • fs_svm() and fs_recursivefeature(handle_categorical = TRUE) use caret’s dummyVars(), which puts a dot between name and level for factors with three or more levels (color.green, color.red) and none for a two-level factor (g1 for factor g with levels "0" and "1").
  • fs_stepwise() keys scores and selected by term, so the factor appears once as color. The per-coefficient values (colorgreen, colorred) are in details$coefficient_scores.
  • fs_mars() attributes each dummy’s importance back to its source predictor and reports color.

Comparing methods

Because every result has the same shape, comparing methods is a loop:

d2 <- data.frame(
  x1 = c(2.1, 3.9, 6.2, 7.8, 10.1, 12.2, 13.8, 16.1, 18.2, 19.9),
  x2 = c(1, 3, 2, 5, 4, 6, 8, 7, 10, 9),
  x3 = c(5, 5, 4, 5, 6, 5, 4, 5, 6, 5),
  y  = c(1.0, 2.1, 2.9, 4.2, 5.0, 6.1, 6.8, 8.1, 9.0, 9.9)
)

runs <- list(
  supervised = fs_supervised(d2, "y", threshold = 0.9),
  infogain   = fs_infogain(d2, "y", top_n = 2)
)
lapply(runs, selected)
#> $supervised
#> [1] "x1" "x2"
#> 
#> $infogain
#> [1] "x1" "x2"

Agreement between methods that work on different principles is weak evidence that a feature matters, and disagreement is a reason to look closer. Neither replaces validating the final set on data that played no part in choosing it; the validation and leakage article shows how.

Empty selections

When nothing passes, selected is character(0). fs_supervised() and fs_unsupervised() also warn that nothing met the criteria; the other functions do not warn about an empty selection. Code that consumes results should handle a length-zero selection:

none <- suppressWarnings(fs_unsupervised(d[, 1:3], threshold = 1e6))
selected(none)
#> character(0)
length(selected(none)) == 0
#> [1] TRUE

An empty selection from a threshold filter usually means the threshold is stricter than every score. summary() still ranks every scored feature, so read the scores there before you choose a new cut. An empty fs_chi() result can also come from Monte Carlo p-values that cannot get below sig_level after the multiple-testing adjustment; featR warns when that happens, and Filter methods explains the fix. If fs_lasso(lambda = "1se") keeps nothing, the default lambda = "min" selects at a smaller penalty and usually keeps more.
